note.question: When does greater consumer eco-sensitivity reduce rather than increase sustainability, and how should durable-goods firms or policymakers respond through pricing, trade-ins, and recycling?
note.overview: The paper is a dynamic monopoly game with forward-looking consumers. The firm chooses prices in two periods while anticipating purchase, delay, and upgrade choices; environmental harm follows endogenously from these strategic responses.

components.label: Subgame-perfect equilibrium of the two-period durable-goods game
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Subgame-perfect equilibrium of the two-period durable-goods game. Section 3.5 explicitly solves the game by backward induction. Consumer indifference conditions generate purchase and upgrade thresholds; the firm first optimizes p_2 and then p_1 while anticipating these thresholds. Lemmas and Propositions 1-5 characterize profit and environmental effects.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: In period 1 the monopolist sets p_1, anticipating period-2 behavior, and consumers either buy product 1 or wait. In period 2 the monopolist sets p_2; prior buyers decide whether to upgrade or keep product 1, and nonbuyers decide whether to buy product 2 or retain the status quo. Eco-sensitivity is absent in period 1 and equals kappa in period 2. The firm solves backward from period 2 and selects p_1 to maximize total two-period profit. a forward-looking seller cannot commit to its future price consumer purchase timing and upgrading are governed by three endogenous thresholds
